items.title: 4.1.8.4 Types of Graphs; Graph Implementation Using Python

source_refs.note: Topic 4.1.8.4 Types of Graphs with 'Graph Implementation Using Python' (PDF 114-116, printed 111-113). Figures 4.11 and 4.12 are replaced by the original diagram with the same edges and weights. The printed code imports matplotlib as 'pit'; corrected to plt.

items: Directed graph: edges have a direction; you can travel from city A to city B only if an edge points that way (Figure 4.11).

blocks.alt: Directed graph of five blue circles A to E with weighted arrows: B to A (10), A to C (12), C to B (20), E to A (7), A to D (60) and C to D (32).
blocks.caption: Figure 4.11: Directed Weighted Graph (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.11).

items: Undirected graph: edges work both ways; if A is friends with B, B is friends with A (Figure 4.12).

blocks.alt: Undirected graph of five circles A, B, C, D and E joined by plain lines: A-B, A-E, B-E, B-D, B-C, C-D and E-D.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.12: Undirected Graph (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.12).

items: Weighted graph: each edge has a weight such as distance, time or cost, which helps find the shortest or quickest route (Figure 4.11).

blocks.title: Python code (each .... is one 4-space indent)
blocks.text:
import networkx as nx
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
G = nx.Graph()          # create a graph
G.add_node("A")
G.add_node("B")
G.add_node("C")
G.add_edge("A", "B")     # add edges
G.add_edge("B", "C")
nx.draw(G, with_labels=True)
plt.show()
The code creates a graph with three nodes and two edges using the NetworkX library and draws it with Matplotlib.
